Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room
Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: Threat items imply an ongoing personal-danger/being-followed formulation, which is hard to reconcile with trauma to a loved one; they read more like direct interpersonal victimization than fear for a loved one.

Within Threat, 'Checking Behind' and 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' reflect hypervigilant danger avoidance, while 'Risky Behavior' points in the opposite direction behaviorally; this combination is possible but clinically strained without any other items supporting disinhibition.

Memory item 'Pain Recall' implies bodily re-experiencing of injury to the patient's own body, which is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one unless she was also directly harmed; the other memory items do not suggest that.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, a prominent risky-behavior item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by fear/avoidance and reliving rather than self-endangering behavior. It pulls the threat profile in a different direction without support from other nodes.

issues.item: Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall in the same body parts as during the event implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma. That is difficult to fit with trauma to a loved one, especially given no other items indicate direct physical victimization.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: The body-focused negative appraisals suggest distrust of one's own injured or trauma-reactive body, which fits direct bodily trauma better than trauma centered on harm to a loved one. In this profile they are not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, 'military topics' is hard to justify unless the loved one’s trauma was specifically military-related; that context is not represented anywhere else in the profile, so this trigger appears mismatched to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room
issues.explanation: 'Locked spaces' suggests a confinement/entrapment trauma context, but the rest of the profile centers on reliving, terror, and generalized danger after trauma to a loved one rather than a personal entrapment event. Without corroborating memory or appraisal content, this trigger looks clinically out of place.

vignette:
Layla, a 63-year-old auditor, sat across from me, her posture rigid, her eyes constantly scanning the room as if searching for an unseen threat. Her life, once meticulously organized and predictable, had been fractured by the unimaginable horror that befell her son, Omar, three years prior. He had been on a solo hiking trip to a remote cabin nestled deep within a national park when he was ambushed. The details that emerged later – his abduction, the makeshift, confined space where he was held, and ultimately, his death – became the anchor of Layla’s present suffering.

In the aftermath, the world became a minefield. Any reminder of the event could instantly bring back the full memory, overwhelming her senses without warning. The scent of pine trees, or the sight of a dense, unkempt patch of woods similar to the park where Omar was taken, now acted as potent triggers. She found herself experiencing full sensory reliving of the horrifying details, the terror on recall as vivid and visceral as the day she received the news. Even being in a small, locked conference room at work, or seeing news reports of other victims, would instantly plunge her back into the nightmare, making her feel as though she was trapped alongside him. The raw power of these triggers, forcing her to relive the trauma, began to solidify her conviction that she was truly helpless and that her body, reacting so violently, had become her enemy. These pervasive triggers didn't just bring back the memories; they also immediately activated a profound sense of threat. This constant, overwhelming sense of imminent danger also had the insidious effect of making her intrusive memories feel even more vivid and inescapable, as if the threat was actively replaying the past. Layla became hypervigilant, perpetually on guard, her body always coiled and ready for danger, which meant she rarely found peace enough to fall or stay asleep.

The relentless onslaught of these experiences began to reshape Layla’s core beliefs. The randomness and brutality of Omar’s death, coupled with her body’s constant state of alarm, led her to believe that she was utterly helpless; she simply couldn't stop bad things from happening to her. This pervasive sense of helplessness, alongside a profound loss of faith in the inherent goodness of people and the safety of life itself, became a heavy burden. Her body, she felt, had become an enemy, constantly reacting as if she were still in danger even when she was objectively safe within her own home. This conviction that her body was betraying her, coupled with her lost faith, only intensified her hypervigilance and made her avoid unfamiliar places, convinced she wouldn't be able to assess the danger lurking there. The memories, particularly the terror on recall, were further amplified by her feeling of helplessness, making them even more agonizing to endure. She found that her constant state of hypervigilance, this relentless scanning for danger, made her even more susceptible to being triggered, causing benign environmental cues like a rustling bush or a closed door to suddenly become deeply unsettling.

The cycle tightened its grip over months. Her pervasive beliefs about her helplessness and lost faith began to actively shape what she perceived as a trigger. A simple picture of a missing person, or even the sound of a distant siren, now felt like a direct assault, confirming her fears and making her more sensitive to these victim memories. The constant threat she felt, the hypervigilance and disrupted sleep, reinforced her negative appraisals, cementing her conviction that her body was indeed an enemy and that she was truly helpless. As an auditor, Layla often had to travel to various client sites, some in more rural areas, or work in small, windowless offices. Her avoidance of unfamiliar places and her heightened vigilance made these assignments increasingly difficult. She started declining engagements, impacting her career and income, the very structure of her predictable life eroding around her. Her sleep problems left her perpetually exhausted, and she became withdrawn, no longer visiting her sister’s cabin by the lake, which was too reminiscent of nature's deceptive calm.

Layla’s life had become one of constant internal battle, her world shrinking with each passing day. The cumulative toll of the terror, the exhaustion, and the growing isolation finally brought her to seek help. What frightened her most was the feeling that she was losing herself, that the world was an irrevocably dangerous place, and that she would never again know peace, only the tightening vise of fear.
